title: Quiz: Xbar-R and Xbar-S Control Charts

questions.text: For a bottling process with x̄̄ = 500g, R̄ = 4g, and n = 5 (A₂ = 0.577), what is the UCL of the Xbar chart?
Why do 3-sigma control limits result in a false alarm rate of approximately 0.27%?
options: Control charts use the t-distribution with 3 degrees of freedom
0.27% was chosen arbitrarily as an industry standard
The 3-sigma rule applies only to the range chart, not the Xbar chart
questions.explanation: From standard normal tables, P(Z > 3) = 0.00135. For a two-sided limit, P(|Z| > 3) = 2 × 0.00135 = 0.0027, or 0.27%.

questions.text: For n = 5 with D₃ = 0 and D₄ = 2.114, a process has R̄ = 5g. What is the LCL of the R chart?
questions.explanation: LCL_R = D₃ × R̄ = 0 × 5 = 0. For small subgroup sizes (n < 7), D₃ = 0, which means the lower control limit is zero — you cannot have a negative range.

questions.text: You observe 9 consecutive subgroup means all above the center line but all within the UCL. According to Western Electric rules, you should:
options: Signal out of control — 8 consecutive points on one side of CL is a rule violation
Take no action — all points are within 3-sigma limits
Widen the control limits to accommodate the pattern
Switch from Xbar-R to Xbar-S to get a better estimate
questions.explanation: Western Electric Rule 4: 8 consecutive points on the same side of the center line signals a process shift, even if no single point exceeds 3σ. The probability of this happening by chance in a stable process is (0.5)^8 = 0.4%.

questions.text: You should switch from an Xbar-R chart to an Xbar-S chart when the subgroup size n is 10 or more.
questions.explanation: For large subgroups (n ≥ 10), the sample standard deviation S is a more statistically efficient estimator of process variability than the range R. The Xbar-S chart uses S̄ with constants A₃, B₃, B₄ instead of A₂, D₃, D₄.
